title: The Emergence of Psychological Safety or its Mirage
authors: Patricia Satterstrom; Michaela Kerrissey
affiliations: New York University, Wagner, New York, New York, United States; Harvard University T H Chan School of Public Health, Health Policy and Management, Boston, Massachusetts, United States
abstract: Leaders often strive to foster psychological safety in teams, and yet it may not emerge. This study builds grounded theory on how psychological safety emerges, or not, on teams. We draw on longitudinal ethnographic data from a matched pair case study of two teams over two years, including verbatim meeting transcripts that elicit the micro-processes affecting psychological safety and interviews that elucidate team members’ interpretations. We identify an illusion initially present on both teams in which surface markers of psychological safety existed but team members nonetheless continued to avoid interpersonal risk—what we call a psychological safety mirage. This occurred because external pressures on leaders spurred them to take self-protective actions that inadvertently reinforced interpersonal risk, despite their continued efforts to invite contributions. One team was eventually able to break from this mirage through a three-phase de-risking process that facilitated psychological safety emergence: (1) collectively recognizing the underlying risk faced by team members, (2) de-risking contributions by offering opportunities to build skills, through which safety was demonstrated and reinforced, and (3) enacting psychological safety, with all team members contributing, reinforcing, and sharing in the benefits of reduced interpersonal risk. This paper advances theory on psychological safety by conceptualizing a team-level de-risking process model that facilitates its emergence and by characterizing its mirage.

title: How Firms Respond to Carbon Taxation
authors: Arzi Adbi; Xiaoteng Wu
affiliations: National University of Singapore Business School, Strategy & Policy, Singapore, Singapore; Peking University Guanghua School of Management, Organization and Strategic Management, Beijing, China
abstract: Although environmental regulations can incentivize firms to reduce emissions, how firms adapt may depend not only on their organizational characteristics but also on the physical realities of their assets. This paper examines how multinational spread, an organizational feature in which firms own and manage similar production activities across countries, and the physical asset characteristics of production facilities jointly shape firms’ responses to carbon taxation. Using global, real-time satellite data on carbon emissions from 882 steel plants across 67 countries over 96 months (January 2015 to December 2022), we analyze operational adjustments firms can make to reduce carbon emissions: producing more cleanly by reducing emissions intensity of production or producing less by reducing asset utilization. We first examine how firms adapt to Canada’s carbon tax using a difference-in-differences (DID) design and then examine the impact of carbon taxes across countries using a stacked DID design. Our analysis reveals that, following Canada’s carbon tax, firms without multinational spread reduce carbon emissions primarily by lowering asset utilization; in contrast, firms with multinational spread additionally reduce emissions intensity of production. Importantly, our analysis of carbon taxes across countries shows that multinational spread alone does not dictate firm adaptation. Adaptation is fundamentally influenced by the physical technology on the ground: firms with multinational spread reduce emissions intensity of production and increase asset utilization at their clean (electric arc furnace) plants relative to dirty plants. Our study thus sheds light on how firms pursue different adaptation strategies at production facilities in response to carbon taxation.

title: Alternating Methods for Large-Scale AC Optimal Power Flow with Unit Commitment
authors: Matthew Brun; Thomas Lee; Dirk Lauinger; Xin Chen; Xu Andy Sun
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Operations Research Center, Cambridge, Massachusetts, 02139-4307, United States; Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Institute for Data, Systems, & Society, Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States; Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Sloan School of Management, Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States; Texas A&M University, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, College Station, Texas, United States; Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Sloan School of Management, Cambridge, Massachusetts, 02142, United States
abstract: Security-constrained unit commitment with alternating current optimal power flow (SCUC-ACOPF) is a central problem in power grid operations that optimizes commitment and dispatch of generators under a physically accurate power transmission model while encouraging robustness against component failures. SCUC-ACOPF requires solving large-scale problems that involve multiple time periods and networks with thousands of buses within strict time limits. In this work, we study a detailed SCUC-ACOPF model with a rich set of features of modern power grids, including price-sensitive load, reserve products, transformer controls, and energy-limited devices. We propose a decomposition scheme and a penalty alternating direction method to find high-quality solutions to this model. Our methodology leverages spatial and temporal decomposition, separating the problem into a set of mixed-integer linear programs for each bus and a set of continuous nonlinear programs for each time period. To improve the performance of the algorithm, we introduce a variety of heuristics, including restrictions of temporal linking constraints, a second-order cone relaxation, and a contingency screening algorithm. We quantify the quality of feasible solutions through a dual bound from a second-order cone program. To evaluate our algorithm, we use large-scale test cases from Challenge 3 of the U.S. Department of Energy s Grid Optimization Competition that resemble real power grid data under a variety of operating conditions and decision horizons. The experiments yield feasible solutions with an average optimality gap of 1.33%, demonstrating that this approach generates near-optimal solutions within stringent time limits.

title: A General Framework for Importance Sampling with Markov Random Walks
authors: Cheng-Der Fuh; Yanwei Jia; Steven Kou
affiliations: Taoyuan, Taiwan; Hong Kong, China; BOSTON UNIVERSITY, Questrom School of Business, Boston, Massachusetts, United States
abstract: Although stochastic models driven by latent Markov processes are widely used, the classical importance sampling methods based on the exponential tilting for these models suffer from difficulties in computing associated eigenvalues and eigenfunctions and the plausibility of the indirect asymptotic large deviation regime for the variance of the estimator. We propose an importance sampling framework that twists the observable and latent processes separately using a link function that directly minimizes the estimator’s variance. An optimal link function is chosen within the locally asymptotically normal family. We show the logarithmic efficiency of the estimator. As applications, we estimate an overflow probability under a pandemic model and the CoVaR, a measurement of the co-dependent financial systemic risk; both are beyond the scope of traditional importance sampling methods due to nonlinear features.

title: The Complexity of Scheduling Pickup and Delivery Jobs
authors: Tianyu Wang; Desheng Wu; David L. Olson
affiliations: Beihang University, School of Economy and Management, Beijing, Beijing, China; UCAS, School of Economy and Management, Beijing, China; Lincoln, United States
abstract: Scheduling pickup and delivery jobs stands as a critical and challenging problem commonly encountered in time-sensitive logistics and transportation. Often, a large number of requests involving shipments from the same location are aggregated into either a fixed number of job queues, referred to as the queueing mode, or into a fixed number of sets, referred to as the pooling mode. Due to the time-sensitive nature, the objective of scheduling jobs by location and routing drivers is to minimize customers’ waiting times. While request aggregation is widely observed in platform economies and related research, the computational complexity of scheduling pickup and delivery jobs has not been studied. This paper presents a comprehensive complexity analysis of this problem. We prove that the problem is strongly NP-hard in the queueing mode, but is polynomially solvable in the pooling mode. Furthermore, we prove that both modes become polynomially solvable when minimizing total distance, as does the queueing mode with fixed number of drivers or scaled-length edges. Finally, we provide approximation guarantees and extend the analysis to bipartite graphs, identifying solvable variants with relaxed map-size constraints to enhance the applicability.

title: Deregulation, Market Structure, and the Evolution of U.S. Banking
authors: Emilio Bisetti; Stephen A. Karolyi; Stefan Lewellen
affiliations: Department of Finance, School of Business and Management, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Clear Water Bay, New Territories, Hong Kong SAR; Department of Finance, Costello College of Business George Mason University, Fairfax, Virginia 22030; Department of Finance, The Pennsylvania State University, State College, Pennsylvania 16802
abstract: We construct novel network-based measures of U.S. state-level bank deregulation intensity that allow us to separately identify the effects of deregulation on competition and investment opportunities. In contrast to existing studies, we find that increased competition leads to higher deposit funding costs and a reduction in banks’ net interest margins and profitability. In response, banks shift their business models and persistently increase their risk taking. Our findings resolve conflicting evidence in the literature and support theories in which reductions in bank charter values lead to higher bank risk taking. This paper was accepted by Camelia Kuhnen, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01128 .

title: Redeploying the Jockeys: The Intermediary Role of Venture Capital in Entrepreneurial Labor Markets
authors: Zhongchen Hu
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen 518172, China
abstract: This paper explores how venture capitalists (VCs) add value by examining their role as labor market intermediaries. Using novel data, I show that VCs create internal labor markets (ILMs) to facilitate entrepreneurial mobility across their portfolio firms. Survey evidence suggests that VCs leverage private information about founders’ abilities to strategically match talent to portfolio firms, creating value for the recipient companies. Consistent with this mechanism of asymmetric learning, I find that (a) former VC partners continue to influence founder mobility, (b) ILM intensity positively predicts VC fund returns, and (c) the ILM effect is stronger when information asymmetry is greater. This paper was accepted by Lin William Cong, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.01626 .

title: Effortful vs. Opportunistic Consumption of Discretionary Time: How Time-Reporting Decisions Influence Extra-Role Effort
authors: Sophie Maussen
affiliations: Department of Accounting, Corporate Finance and Taxation, Ghent University, 9000 Ghent, Belgium
abstract: Employees often work under incomplete contracts, performing both contracted in-role tasks and valuable but noncontracted extra-role activities. Once employees have completed in-role tasks, discretionary time remains, which they may allocate to extra-role activities or consume opportunistically. This study examines how managers’ time-reporting decisions, as a less intrusive form of control, affect subordinates’ effort-allocation decisions. I propose two opposing predictions. First, managers’ control implementations may signal distrust, resulting in more opportunism and thus less extra-role effort. Second, I identify value signaling as a novel theoretical mechanism through which time-reporting decisions may increase extra-role effort. The main experiment manipulated two factors: the type of time report (aggregated versus disaggregated) and its implementation source (managerial choice versus random assignment) to isolate signaling effects from monitoring effects. Results reveal that when managers choose not to implement disaggregated time reporting—that is, reports that make discretionary time salient—subordinates significantly reduce their extra-role effort. Structural equation modeling shows that value signaling outweighs distrust signaling in driving employees’ effort-allocation decisions. In contrast, when the time-reporting format is randomly assigned, effort remains unchanged, underscoring the signaling role of managerial choice. An additional online experiment shows directionally consistent results with the main experiment. These findings reveal a hidden cost of not controlling and contribute to the literature on incomplete contracts, slack resources, and input-based controls in modern work contexts. This paper was accepted by Ranjani Krishnan, accounting. Funding: This work was supported by the Bijzonder Onderzoeksfonds UGent [Grant BOF/STA/202009/047]. Supplemental Material: The data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00955 .

title: The Workplace GenAI Usage Divide: A Genetics-Informed Cognitive and Metacognitive Account
authors: Shuhua Sun; Shiyang Gong; Yinliang (Ricky) Tan
affiliations: Tulane University Freeman School of Business, Management, New Orleans, Louisiana, United States; Beijing Normal University, Business School, Beijing, China; China Europe International Business School, Freeman School of Business, Shanghai, China
abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly deployed in organizations, yet employees differ substantially and persistently in how frequently and intensively they use it. This workplace “usage divide” raises a fundamental but underexplored question: Why do employees differ systematically in their use of GenAI, even under common formal access? We argue that this divide reflects a broader challenge for IS research: explaining the use of systems that are probabilistic rather than deterministic, and general-purpose yet uneven and evolving in their capabilities. In workplaces where employees remain accountable for task performance, these properties make the use of GenAI not a routine adoption decision but a judgment process in which employees assess the system’s credibility and determine where task-relevant expertise lies. Drawing on molecular genetics and metacognition research, we theorize that genetic propensity, indexed by the educational attainment polygenic score (PGS)—an aggregate genetic index associated with educational attainment—helps account for systematic variation in these judgments and, ultimately, persistent differences in workplace GenAI use. Specifically, we develop a parsimonious two-pathway model linking educational attainment PGS to GenAI use: a cognitive pathway involving formal educational attainment and perceptions of GenAI credibility, and a metacognitive pathway involving strategic mindset and metaknowledge of where task-relevant expertise lies. We test our model using a multisource dataset combining primary genetic data, survey measures, and 21 months of objective usage logs. The results show that educational attainment PGS, a broad distal genetic index, is associated with both GenAI use frequency and interaction intensity and provide theory-consistent evidence for the proposed pathways. Overall, our study offers a micro-foundational account of the persistent GenAI usage divide and advances IS theory on the use of probabilistic, general-purpose systems in the workplace.

title: Spatial Competition in Fast-Charging Networks
authors: Philipp Artur Artur Kienscherf; Yixin Lu; Long He; Wolfgang Ketter
affiliations: University of Cologne, Faculty of Management, Economics and Social Sciences, Koln, Nordrhein-Westfalen, Germany; The George Washington University, School of Business, Washington, District of Columbia, United States; University of Notre Dame Mendoza College of Business, Information Technology, Analytics, and Operations, Notre Dame, Indiana, United States
abstract: Despite the steady growth of fast-charging networks under government subsidies, the impact of spatial and ownership structures of charging points on pricing strategies of charging point operators (CPOs) and consumer welfare is poorly understood. Given EVs’ limited range, the competition in a fast-charging network is inherently regional. It is unclear whether and under what circumstances CPOs’ competition can lead to regional monopoly, which may hinder the transition to electric mobility. In this paper, we develop a novel framework to examine the competitive dynamics in fast-charging networks that serve regional demand, incorporating delay costs arising from congestion and locational attractiveness of charging stations. At the core of our framework is a spatial competition model, which characterizes the strategic interactions between CPOs and consumers. To overcome tractability issues associated with large networks that arise from real-world settings, we propose a computationally efficient method to optimize CPOs’ pricing decisions. We instantiate the framework in Germany’s Deutschlandnetz, whose awarded regional network comprises 900 charging stations. Using demand projections for 2030, we conduct a series of counterfactual simulations. Our analysis generates four sets of findings. First, price exhibits a strong negative correlation with the local competitiveness level (measured by the density of charging stations), but shows no clear dependence on absolute demand levels. Second, CPOs’ profits are shaped by both local competitiveness and absolute demand. Third, a uniform, stringent price cap may create inefficiencies in network utilization and discourage infrastructure investment, particularly in less lucrative regions. Finally, spatial and ownership constraints in tender rules may fail to ensure competitive outcomes in large-scale charging networks, allowing CPOs to strategically select locations that strengthen their market power ex post. Taken together, these findings suggest that policymakers should enable regionally equitable access to fast charging while ensuring efficient network utilization.

title: Multimarket Contact and Long-Term Oriented Language in Competition
authors: He Gao; Tieying Yu; Hyun-Soo Woo; Albert A. Cannella
affiliations: University of Delaware; Boston College; The University of Mississippi; Texas A&M University
abstract: Corporate disclosure has long served as a strategic tool for managing the perceptions of audiences that shape a firm’s access to resources. Prior research has largely focused on why firms use disclosure to engage capital-market constituents such as investors and analysts, leaving open the question of when and why firms disclose for competitive purposes. Focusing on the temporal orientation of competitive strategy communication, we examine how multimarket contact (MMC) shapes firms’ use of long-term oriented language (LTL). We argue that greater MMC raises the risk of cross-market retaliation, strengthening firms’ incentives to signal a restrained competitive posture through LTL, particularly when competitive capacity is visibly constrained by poor financial performance or analyst downgrade revisions. Using a sample of 36 U.S. manufacturing firms across six industries from 2015 to 2024, we find evidence generally consistent with our predictions.

title: Healing As Organizing in Solidarity Spaces: An Affective Perspective on Post-disaster Recovery
authors: Chaïma Sophia Benzekri
abstract: This paper examines how community-led solidarity initiatives enable healing in the aftermath of disaster. Drawing on a two-year qualitative study in post-explosion Beirut, it explores how solidarity spaces function as relational structures of repair – sites where material response and affective recovery are not separate processes but mutually constitutive ones. While post-disaster organizing research has emphasized resource mobilization and agility, and disaster studies has identified the importance of community-led recovery, neither has fully explored how organizing enables healing to unfold collectively. Addressing this gap, the study makes two contributions. First, it reframes solidarity spaces as generative holding environments: relational infrastructures that simultaneously contain suffering and enable the emergence of new social arrangements. Second, it conceptualizes healing as organizing: a distributed, collective, and enacted process through which communities transform suffering into agency. Healing, in this account, is not an individual psychological process nor an outcome that follows organizing; it is the very practice through which recovery unfolds, as participants become agents of their own material and affective transformation through acts of solidarity.

title: Consider the Dashboard: Exploring a visual medium of datafication
authors: Felix Diefenhardt
abstract: Dashboards are central to contemporary organizations aiming to ‘datafy’ decision making and management practices. As one of the primary media through which people engage with digital data in organizational contexts, dashboards shape how data is accessed and perceived. Despite their ubiquity, there is limited understanding of how dashboards mediate data visibility and influence observers’ perceptions of the data. Drawing on theories of mediation and diagrammatics, this paper analyzes the ‘generic form’ shared by all dashboards. It then identifies the modes of observation encouraged by dashboards, revealing how they position their observers. While grounded in theoretical arguments, the analysis incorporates empirical examples from a study on the datafication of Human Resource Management. The paper makes two key contributions. It emphasizes the critical role of visual forms in datafication processes, and it highlights the organizational implications of the use of a specific kind of visual medium: the dashboard.

title: Black pragmatism and organization studies
authors: Jared M. Poole
abstract: I argue for Black pragmatism’s usefulness to organization studies by intervening in debates about the normative foundations of stakeholder theory. Tracing three braided themes within Black pragmatism (tragicomic hope, critical temper, and democratic faith), I show how they both illuminate neglected aspects of the pragmatist themes of inquiry, abduction, and community that have influenced organization studies and extend those concepts to open new avenues of inquiry. I suggest that Black pragmatism reveals how the libertarian assumptions of stakeholder theory are inconsistent with its pragmatist commitments, and that this weakness even applies to recent attempts to center stakeholder theory upon marginalized stakeholders.

title: Street Fights and Court Battles: Incumbent mobilization and the timing of regulatory bans against platform entrants
authors: Bilgehan Uzunca; Pinar Ozcan
abstract: In this paper, we examine how incumbent-led mobilization against Uber’s platform entry in Europe relates to regulatory bans, public attention, and consumer-side uptake. Combining hand-coded data on taxi-sector tactics and frames with first regulatory bans, Uber app downloads, and Google search interest across 22 European countries from 2012 to 2020, we identify a differentiated temporal pattern. Private tactics are strongly associated with first-ban hazard in the short window following mobilization, whereas lawsuits are positively associated over a longer window. The frames incumbents deploy also matter: legitimacy-challenge frames portraying UberPop as incompatible with lawful and fair competition are more consistently associated with bans than compliance-dispute frames focused on tax or labor obligations. At the same time, private tactics and lawsuits coincide with immediate increases in app downloads and Google search interest, indicating an attention spillover from incumbent contestation. Lawsuit-related download elevations display marginally greater persistence than those associated with private tactics, although this difference is not stronger early after entry. Taken together, the findings show that incumbent mobilization in platform markets can be associated with regulatory bans and consumer-side uptake of the entrants they seek to exclude at the same time. The results establish temporal association, although the direction of influence within this process cannot be isolated.

title: Patience and Organization Studies: Festina lente
authors: Mark van Vuuren; Boris H. J. M. Brummans
abstract: Modern organizations often valorize speed and immediacy, treating acceleration as the dominant temporal logic of organizational life. Challenging this logic remains difficult, however, because organization studies lacks a well-developed conceptual language for alternative ways of engaging with time. We propose patience as one such alternative. Building on recent work on Eigenzeit, we argue that organizations can partially uncouple from external temporal pressures and develop forms of relative temporal autonomy that enable the orchestration of differentiated temporalities. While Eigenzeit highlights how organizations establish and sustain a temporality of their own amid complex temporal demands, less attention has been paid to the pacing through which this temporality is enacted in everyday organizational life. We therefore foreground pacing as the practical means by which organizations enact and sustain their own temporality. Within this context, patience emerges as a particular mode of pacing grounded in purposeful deceleration. To make this mode of pacing analytically visible, we identify four manifestations of organizational patience: waiting, restraining, forbearing, and persisting. Drawing on insights from the sociology of time, organization studies, and philosophy, we show how these manifestations represent distinct ways of pacing organizational activities by holding time open, delaying intervention, staying with difficulty, and sustaining engagement over time. By reframing patience as a distinctive mode of pacing rather than passive inactivity, we show how organizations cultivate and sustain an Eigenzeit through practices that contribute to the orchestration of competing temporal demands. This perspective advances organization studies by illuminating how temporal orchestration is accomplished through everyday organizational interactions and how patience enables organizations to sustain resilience and meaningful engagement in the face of acceleration pressures.

title: EXPRESS: The Effect of State-Mandated Employment Certificates on Child Labor Violations in the United States
authors: Jiacong (Fred) Bao; Ashish Kabra
abstract: The number of minors involved in child labor violations in the United States more than tripled from 2017 to 2025. Compounding this issue, several state legislatures have recently weakened child labor protection laws. A key component of these laws is whether employers are required to obtain an employment certificate when hiring minors under 18 years of age, which typically requires a parent’s signature and is issued by a school. Proponents of loosening child labor regulations argue that there is a lack of evidence demonstrating the effectiveness of these laws in reducing child labor violations. In this study, we examine the effect of state-mandated employment certificates on reducing child labor violations. We find that the requirement leads to an average of 13.3% fewer violation cases (not statistically significant), 31.8% fewer minors involved in child labor violations, and 34.9% lower civil penalties per minor, indicating reduced severity of violations that do occur. The negative effects on the number of cases and minors persist after addressing endogeneity concerns, as assessed using two novel instrumental variables. Furthermore, we find a positive relationship between the number of unaccompanied migrant children released to a state and the incidence and severity of child labor violations, suggesting that this demographic is particularly vulnerable to labor exploitation. We identify two key mechanisms driving the effectiveness of employment certificates. First, they act as a legal deterrent for employers, as the documented acknowledgment of regulations makes it more difficult to claim ignorance. This is reflected in the higher rate of violations categorized as “willful” in certificate-mandate states. Second, they enhance stakeholder awareness and monitoring. Compliance improves for requirements explicitly documented in the certificates but not for those less visible. Moreover, among common certificate features, parental consent shows the strongest protective effect, suggesting the importance of active oversight and awareness. To our knowledge, this study is the first to provide quantitative evidence for the efficacy of mandating employment certificates in reducing child labor violations. It highlights the critical role of state policies in protecting minor workers and aims to enrich the discourse on child labor regulation and policy implementation.

title: Exploration Across Incompatible Technologies: How Firms Organize Flexibility for Innovation
authors: Yong H. Kim; Ziyi Chen; Chang Hyun Kim; Toby Li
affiliations: Mays Business School Texas A&M University College Station Texas USA; Faculty of Business and Economics The University of Melbourne Carlton Victoria Australia; China Europe International Business School Shanghai People's Republic of China
abstract: ABSTRACT Firms often face multiple emerging technologies that evolve in parallel yet share limited architectural compatibility. In such settings, firms may concentrate innovation on one trajectory or pursue flexibility by maintaining engagement across multiple trajectories. We theorize that flexibility can improve innovation performance, but that these benefits depend on organizational structures that facilitate deep, trajectory‐specific learning and effective coordination. We argue that focused subsidiaries enable deep expertise within individual technologies, external collaborations provide access to complementary expertise beyond firm boundaries, and organizational modularity reduces the coordination burdens associated with pursuing multiple trajectories. Using 40‐year longitudinal data from the flat‐panel display industry, we find that the benefits of a flexibility strategy for innovation performance are substantially greater when firms have more focused subsidiaries, engage in more external collaboration, or exhibit higher organizational modularity. These findings are consistent across three complementary dimensions of innovation performance: patent impact, patent monetary value, and new product introductions. When these organizational arrangements are limited, the relationship between flexibility and innovation performance is substantially weaker. Our study demonstrates how organizational design enables firms to realize the innovation benefits of flexibility across architecturally incompatible technological trajectories.

title: On the front line: An appraisal and an invitation
authors: Gerbrand Tholen
affiliations: Department of Sociology, City St George’s, University of London, UK
abstract: This editorial marks 17 years of the On the Front Line (OtFL) section in Work, Employment and Society (WES), to reflect on its distinctive contribution to the sociology of work. It traces the section’s major thematic strands, including precarity and insecurity, gender and identity, collective action, care work and race and racism. It further identifies storytelling, emotional depth and reduced analytical mediation as the section’s defining qualities, illustrated through accounts of in-work poverty, NHS burnout and truck driving. The editorial closes by inviting new contributions.

title: AI and Stress
authors: Thang Dang; Phuong Huynh
affiliations: Department of Economics University of Turku Turku Finland; University of Economics Ho Chi Minh City (UEH) Ho Chi Minh City Vietnam; University of Turku Turku Finland
abstract: ABSTRACT Given the spread of artificial intelligence (AI) tools at work, understanding their health implications is critically important. We use rich survey data from Finland and apply propensity score matching that accounts for observable differences between regular AI users and non‐users to estimate the relationship between reported AI usage at work and workers’ reported stress. Regular AI use is associated with a 4.4 percentage point higher probability of reporting stress, equivalent to a 25.6% increase relative to baseline. Comparing two competing explanations, we find that this pattern is more consistent with heavier work demands than with concerns about job loss: AI use is associated with more unpaid work outside working hours and, less precisely, with intense work absorption, but not with job insecurity. Exploratory subgroup estimates are larger and individually significant for men, non‐supervisors, unionized workers and employees in medium‐sized workplaces, although the differences across subgroups are not statistically significant.

title:
Explaining Coexisting Trust and Distrust Transitions: The Case of Senior Doctors in the
                    <scp>UK NHS</scp>
authors: Branko Božič; Stacey Bushfield; Graeme Martin
affiliations: NEOMA Business School; Edinburgh Napier University Business School; University of Dundee School of Business
abstract: Abstract The emergence of distrust in organizations damages working relationships and leads to poor organizational performance. We examine how senior doctors in the UK NHS transitioned from low trust/low distrust to low trust/high distrust in their managers and employer. Drawing on qualitative data from three time periods, we show, counter‐intuitively, how a positive crisis response by doctors' leaders during COVID‐19 intensified a long‐term downward trust–distrust trajectory. This response temporarily restored confidence and elevated expectations of a renewed psychological contract among doctors. When those expectations were later violated, scepticism and value incongruence grew, inciting negative expectations and a descent into distrust. We make three contributions to trust–distrust theory. First, we identify a previously unexplained pathway from coexisting low trust/low distrust to low trust/high distrust through a temporary state of high trust/low distrust. Second, we explain how ideological contract violations, perceived betrayals of core values and professional identities, drive the development of distrust. Third, we extend punctuated‐threshold explanations of distrust emergence by demonstrating that distrust can arise not only from accumulating negative experiences but also from the collapse of newly restored positive expectations. This has broader implications for the leadership of change, particularly the management of hope and expectations during crisis.

title: Constant Connectivity as Everyday Practice: Theorizing Through Problematization
authors: Matthew B. Perrigino; Roshni Raveendhran; Ji Woon Ryu
affiliations: Baruch College; University of Virginia; Portland State University
abstract: Abstract Despite a significant amount of research on constant connectivity , defined as the opportunity to remain connected to work at any time, from any place, we assert that there remains a disconnect between how constant connectivity is studied and how it unfolds in everyday occurrences. Using the miner‐prospector continuum, we problematize the extant literature to evaluate this assertion and develop new theory. Our mining reveals that constant connectivity studies rely on notions of time and place that insufficiently demarcate work–nonwork boundaries; prescribe constant connectivity as either wholly incompatible with enacting nonwork roles or inherently interfering with specific nonwork activities; and operationalize constant connectivity with vague ‘technology use’ constructs. In prospecting, we conceptualize constant connectivity as a set of sociomaterial practices that capture how: technology affords opportunities to engage in, and disengage from, work activity; constant connectivity and nonwork role enactment are compatible via the pursuit of work and nonwork activities in parallel or sequentially; and work–nonwork boundaries are socially constructed in ways that transcend time and place. Taken together, we extend considerations of constant connectivity beyond knowledge workers to any occupation (skilled trades; physical labour) in which individuals use technology to conduct aspects of work at any time, from any place.

title: Backmatter of Quantitative Economics Vol. 17 Iss. 4
Frontmatter of Quantitative Economics Vol. 17 Iss. 4
Worker‐side discrimination: Beliefs and preferences
authors: Md Moshi Ul Alam; Mehreen Mookerjee; Sanket Roy
affiliations: Department of Economics, Clark University; College of Interdisciplinary Studies, Zayed University; School of Business Administration, Department of Economics, American University of Sharjah
abstract: When agents choose among options with unobserved attributes to maximize expected utility, their choices conflate preferences with beliefs about those attributes. We develop a novel theory‐driven identification strategy for such settings, showing that compensating differentials separately identify beliefs from preferences. Noting that workers' preferences and beliefs shape labor market outcomes, yet remain understudied, we apply our method to provide the first evidence on the distribution of workers' preferences over manager gender, and their beliefs about managers' mentoring ability. In the absence of information on manager mentoring ability, workers are indifferent to manager gender. However, upon receiving information on manager mentorship ability, workers prefer to work for female managers, willing to forgo 1.7% of average annual wages. Hence, absent additional information, workers believe female managers are worse mentors (1.6% wage equivalent). Nonparametric estimates of the distributions reveal that 76% prefer female managers with mentoring information, and 67% believe male managers are better mentors absent information. Machine learning algorithms show that individuals with higher education are less likely to hold such beliefs. These beliefs are primarily driven by perceptions that women are less competent. Evidence suggests these beliefs are biased, highlighting scope for information‐based policy interventions.

title: Finite‐state Markov chain approximations: A hidden Markov approach
authors: Eva F. Janssens; Sean McCrary
affiliations: Department of Economics, University of Michigan; Department of Economics, The Ohio State University
abstract: This paper proposes a novel finite‐state Markov chain approximation method for Markov processes with continuous support, providing both an optimal grid and a transition probability matrix. The method can be used for multivariate processes and processes with time‐varying components. It is based on minimizing the information loss between a hidden Markov model and the true data‐generating process. We provide sufficient conditions under which this information loss can be made arbitrarily small, provided enough grid points are used. We compare our method to existing methods through the lens of an asset‐pricing model and a life‐cycle consumption‐savings model. We find that our method can lead to more parsimonious discretizations and more accurate solutions, and that the discretization matters for the welfare costs of risk, marginal propensities to consume, and the amount of wealth inequality a life‐cycle model can generate.

title: Intrahousehold inequality and savings in retirement
authors: Minsu Chang; Ami Ko
affiliations: Department of Economics, Seoul National University; Department of Economics, Georgetown University
abstract: The distribution of resources between spouses and the extent to which household savings reflect each spouse's motives are fundamental to analyzing married retirees' welfare. We provide one of the first quantitative assessments of intrahousehold inequality in bargaining power and its implications for consumption allocation during marriage, savings, and welfare in old age. To do so, we estimate a dynamic collective model of retired couples with individual‐specific preferences and relative bargaining power, in which spouses jointly choose consumption, saving, care arrangements, and housing in the face of health and mortality shocks. We find that wives' mean consumption shares are close to parity in retirement, although there is substantial dispersion. We also find meaningful gender differences in saving motives and preferences: wives have stronger precautionary motives due to their longer life expectancy and higher long‐term care risk, while men exhibit greater bequest motives toward children. Consequently, our estimated collective model shows that reforms to old‐age social insurance have different welfare effects for wives and husbands, revealing distributional consequences that would be obscured under a unitary framework.

title: Fertility, child gender, and parental migration decision: Evidence from China
authors: Zibin Huang; Lin Lin; Junsen Zhang
affiliations: College of Business, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics; School of Labor and Human Resources, Renmin University of China; School of Economics, Zhejiang University
abstract: We study how the number and gender of children affect rural‐to‐urban parental migration in China. Exploiting variation from the “1.5‐child policy,” which allowed a second birth only if the first‐born was a girl, we separately identify the causal effects of fertility and child gender based on a novel semiparametric method. Using the 2010 population census, we find that an additional child increases the likelihood of joint parental migration by 12.1%, while the presence of a son raises it by a further 11.6%. These comparable magnitudes show that gender matters as much as fertility in shaping migration decisions. The results suggest that the higher financial demands of larger families—especially those with boys—outweigh the emotional costs of separation, motivating parents to migrate. Traditional IV estimates would be severely downward biased if only the number of children were considered.

title: A nonparametric test for diurnal variation in spot correlation processes
authors: Kim Christensen; Ulrich Hounyo; Zhi Liu
affiliations: Department of Economics and Business Economics, Aarhus University; Center for Research in Energy: Economics and Markets (CoRE), Aarhus University; Danish Finance Institute (DFI); Department of Economics, University at Albany, State University of New York; Department of Mathematics, Faculty of Science and Technology, University of Macau
abstract: The association between log‐price increments of exchange‐traded equities, as measured by their spot correlation estimated from high‐frequency data, exhibits a pronounced upward‐sloping and almost piecewise linear relationship at the intraday horizon. There is notably lower—on average less positive—correlation in the morning than in the afternoon. We develop a nonparametric testing procedure to detect such variation in a correlation process. The test statistic has a known distribution under the null hypothesis, whereas it diverges under the alternative. We run a Monte Carlo simulation to discover the finite sample properties of the test statistic, which are close to the large sample predictions, even for small sample sizes and realistic levels of diurnal variation. In an application, we implement the test on a high‐frequency dataset covering the stock market over an extended period. The test leads to rejection of the null most of the time. This suggests diurnal variation in the correlation process is a nontrivial effect in practice. We show how conditioning information about macroeconomic news and corporate earnings announcements affects the intraday correlation curve.

title: Finite‐sample auction inference using transaction prices
authors: David M. Kaplan; Xin Liu
affiliations: Department of Economics, University of Missouri; School of Economic Sciences, Washington State University
abstract: We first provide inference on the quantile function of the bid distribution in first‐price or descending auctions, and the quantile function of the value distribution in second‐price or ascending auctions, with a known number of bidders with symmetric independent private values. Specifically, we provide finite‐sample, nonparametric, tuning parameter‐free, uniform confidence bands for these quantile functions when observing only the transaction price. We also show how these bands can be used to construct confidence intervals for many counterfactuals and economic quantities that are functionals of the value distribution. Some confidence intervals inherit the same properties of our bands, besides having conservative instead of exact coverage, while others require asymptotic arguments and/or tuning parameters. Even if the observed number of bidders varies across auctions, our bands' finite‐sample coverage is exact, assuming exogenous participation. With a fixed number of bidders, we also derive uniform confidence bands robust to auction‐level unobserved heterogeneity. This includes new partial identification results that bound the bid or value quantile function in terms of the transaction price quantile function. Empirically, our new methodology is applied to timber auction data to examine heterogeneity across appraisal value and number of bidders, which helps assess the combination of symmetric independent private values and exogenous participation, and to provide confidence intervals for the optimal reserve price and the economic benefit of running the auction instead of a random lottery.

title: School choice, skill measures, and graduation
authors: María Elena Ortega-Hesles; Marco Pariguana
affiliations: Independent researcher; WZB Berlin Social Science Center
abstract: This paper studies the effects of combining skill measures to construct the priority order in a centralized education market. We use data from Mexico City, where seat rationing relies solely on a one‐shot exam score. We first show that admission to the most oversubscribed schools decreases graduation among marginally admitted students, but this effect is heterogeneous. It decreases with the one‐shot exam score among inframarginal students and is negative for marginal students with low GPAs but null for those with high GPAs. We then use a model of school choice and graduation to study the equity and efficiency of counterfactual priority orders that combine the one‐shot exam score and GPA. Greater weight on GPA increases access to the most oversubscribed schools for girls and low‐SES students. However, assigning roughly equal weight to both skill measures maximizes their graduation rates at these schools.

title: Decomposing the rise in markups
authors: Has Vlokhoven
affiliations: Department of Economics, Tilburg University
abstract: A recent literature argues that the rise in aggregate markups is due to economic activity reallocating toward high‐markup firms rather than an increase in firm‐level markups. I show that standard decomposition methods used to analyze this phenomenon can estimate a nonzero reallocation effect even when the joint distribution of markups and market shares is time‐invariant. This is due to churning in the firm‐level distribution of markups and market shares. Empirically, I find that a large and positive reallocation effect is found by standard decomposition methods when the distribution is time‐invariant. I propose a new decomposition, which gives that the rise in the aggregate markup mainly comes from changes in the markup distribution rather than changes in the market share distribution.

title: Standard errors when a regressor is randomly assigned
authors: Denis Chetverikov; Jinyong Hahn; Zhipeng Liao; Andres Santos
affiliations: Department of Economics, University of California, Los Angeles
abstract: We show that the OLS variance formula simplifies when values of the regressor of interest are assigned randomly and independently of other regressors. When the regressor of interest is independent not only of other regressors but also of the error term, the homoscedastic variance formula is valid even if regression errors are correlated. When the error term is heteroscedastic with respect to the regressor of interest, the variance formula has to be adjusted not only for heteroscedasticity but also for correlation structure of the error term. However, even in the latter case, some simplifications are possible.

title: Identification of daily oil price shocks and their uncertainties via conditional heteroskedasticity
authors: Shu Wang
affiliations: Chair of Econometrics, University of Göttingen
abstract: This paper develops a daily structural VAR for identifying oil price shocks from conditional heteroskedasticity and quantifies the transmission of their time‐varying uncertainty. Identification exploits volatility clustering and spillovers in a structural GARCH specification and the complete identified set is derived. We derive covariance impulse response functions and introduce a time‐varying forecast error variance decomposition (TV‐FEVD) that allows for a decomposition of short‐horizon forecast uncertainty across episodes. We study the asymptotic properties of a two‐step quasi‐maximum likelihood estimator and demonstrate via extensive simulations the robustness of the estimator across a wide range of data‐generating distributions. Empirically, the model identifies three daily shocks with distinct first‐ and second‐order transmission. TV‐FEVD shows that oil‐price forecast uncertainty in early 2020 shifted from aggregate business‐cycle uncertainty, as pandemic news affected expected economic conditions, to oil‐market tightness risk during the Saudi–Russia price war and production cuts.

title: Whether and when: Women's work, birth spacing, and parity progression in late‐nineteenth‐century Derbyshire
authors: Emma Diduch
affiliations: Cambridge Group for the History of Population and Social Structure, Department of Geography University of Cambridge Cambridge UK
abstract: Abstract Women's labour force participation features prominently in discussions of low birth rates and the Second Demographic Transition, and has also been hypothesized to have played a role in falling marital fertility during the First Demographic Transition. Historical data have been lacking, however, to assess these theories robustly and to distinguish between the effects of women's work on birth intervals and parity progression. This paper uses a split‐population cure model to analyse stopping and spacing by couples in late‐nineteenth‐century Derbyshire, using linked census data to demonstrate the association between women's occupations before marriage and subsequent marital fertility. Combining these linked census records and the 1911 census fertility survey, complete birth histories have been reconstructed for women who married from the 1880s onwards. The results suggest that couples in this period were controlling their fertility from the beginning of marriage via a combination of stopping and spacing, and that spacing births played a greater role in the low fertility of female textile workers than it did amongst some other occupational groups. These results provide more concrete evidence for the importance of women's labour force participation and birth spacing during the fertility transition in England and Wales.

title: Editorial Board
Climate Risk Disclosure and Risk Sharing in Financial Markets
authors: Kevin Smith
abstract: Abstract In this paper, I model how climate risk disclosure impacts climate risk sharing among investors. I show that this disclosure can improve risk sharing by helping investors identify stocks that effectively hedge climate risk, and I analyze the disclosure’s impact on investors’ equilibrium portfolio choices. I then study firms’ voluntary disclosure incentives and analyze when disclosure mandates enhance risk sharing. Finally, I demonstrate that, by facilitating risk sharing, climate risk disclosure reduces the climate risk premium among stocks held by climate-focused investors. Hence, disclosure can lower the valuations of firms with low climate exposures and the overall market. (JEL: D82, D84, G12, G14)

title: Government Guarantees and Dynamic Debt Runs
authors: Jacopo Magnani; Yabin Wang
affiliations: Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) , Department of Economics
abstract: Abstract This study quantifies the impact of public guarantees on the stability of bank wholesale funding. We study the Chinese market for negotiable certificates of deposit (NCDs) around the first bank failure in two decades, the Baoshang event, which struck investors’ belief in government guarantees on wholesale bank debt. We document a sharp increase in NCD spreads, issuance failures, and runs, with weaker banks becoming more exposed to rollover risk after the event. Using a model of dynamic debt runs, we estimate that the perceived guarantee fell from 54% of creditor losses before the event to approximately zero after the event. The decline is largest for small banks, low-rated banks, and rural commercial banks. Our structural model also allows us to compare alternative policies aimed at stabilizing creditors’ willingness to roll over short-term debt.

title: The Added Bonus of Foreign Investments: Global Mutual Funds and Multinational Firm Returns
authors: Wei Jiao
affiliations: Rutgers School of Business‐Camden Rutgers University
abstract: Abstract This paper uses global mutual funds to study foreign information dissemination across countries into multinationals’ stock prices. To invest internationally, these funds collect information from foreign countries where they invest. Such foreign information helps funds invest in U.S. multinationals operating in those same foreign countries. Global funds overweight and outperform on the selected multinationals’ stocks. They exploit market‐level, industry‐level, and firm‐specific foreign information. The trading activities of these funds accelerate the incorporation of foreign information into the selected multinationals’ prices. Our findings suggest that global mutual funds are important mechanisms for information dissemination into multinationals’ asset prices in global markets.
journal: Journal of Money, Credit and Banking

title:
Liquidity, Collateral Quality, and Interest Rates
                    <sup>a</sup>
authors: JUNG‐HYUN AHN; VINCENT BIGNON; RÉGIS BRETON; ANTOINE MARTIN
abstract: Abstract This paper analyzes how collateral quality shocks affect banks' liquidity management and the risk‐free rate. We develop a model where banks manage liquidity through near‐cash assets and marketable securities subject to idiosyncratic and/or aggregate shocks. Collateral quality deterioration leads to nonmonotonic changes in liquidity holdings: moderate declines reduce cash holdings via lower market returns, while severe declines cause precautionary hoarding and market freezes. Reduced collateral quality depresses the risk‐free rate. Liquidity regulation and negative interest rate policies can mitigate these effects. Our findings highlight the risks of collateral quality shocks and the importance of policy complementarities in addressing liquidity issues.

title: The Role of Supply Chains in Climate Disclosure
authors: Pietro Bonetti; Yang (Ellen) EN; Igor Kadach; Gaizka Ormazabal
affiliations: IESE Business School; IESE Business School, CEPR, & ECGI
abstract: ABSTRACT We examine the role of supply chains in shaping the public disclosure of climate information. We leverage a unique empirical setting enabled by CDP—the leading platform for corporate climate risk reporting—which allows customers to demand climate‐related information from their suppliers. Using a large international sample of customer–supplier pairs, we find a positive association between customers’ information demand and suppliers’ public disclosure on the CDP. While the estimated association is modest on average, it exhibits substantial cross‐sectional variation reflecting the disclosure incentives of both customers and suppliers as well as their relative bargaining power. We also find descriptive evidence consistent with one potential implication of the documented association for corporate decision‐making: shifts in supply network relationships toward greener and more transparent suppliers. Overall, our findings contribute to ongoing debates on how to foster climate disclosure.

title: Intertemporal Dynamics of Cost Asymmetry
authors: Eti Einhorn; Efrat Shust
affiliations: Coller School of Management Tel Aviv University Tel Aviv‐Yafo Israel; The Department of Management and Economics The Open University of Israel Ra'anana Israel
abstract: ABSTRACT We study the intertemporal dynamics of asymmetric cost behavior in a competitive setting. Our analysis delves into the primitives of cost asymmetry and explores its dynamic evolution over time. The analysis yields the result that cost behavior is asymmetric by default and path‐dependent, transpiring as cost stickiness following prior resource expansion and taking the form of cost anti‐stickiness after previous resource contraction. The analysis further suggests that the magnitude of cost asymmetry, either stickiness or anti‐stickiness, is decreasing in demand uncertainty and competition intensity, increasing in adjustment costs and time discounting, and greater for small demand shocks than for large demand shocks. By highlighting cost asymmetry as a dynamic, rather than static, phenomenon, and by providing new, testable predictions regarding the direction and magnitude of cost asymmetry across firms and over time, our results offer theoretical grounding for the empirical cost asymmetry literature and may also help investors and other stakeholders interpret cost behavior in light of firms' recent history of expansion or contraction and their competitive environment.

title: America's most “far‐reaching institution”: The work and legacies of the Freedmen's Bureau
authors: Michael Albertus; Jon Rogowski
affiliations: Professor, Department of Political Science University of Chicago Chicago Illinois USA
abstract: Abstract Reconstruction was the American state's first sustained peacetime intervention into local communities, and the Freedmen's Bureau was its most important component. What was the social impact of this program? Using an original data set on Freedmen's Bureau operations, we link the distribution and duration of Bureau offices to local socioeconomic outcomes. We find that the Bureau had positive effects for both Black and White residents of counties that hosted offices. Moreover, these effects were accompanied by the development of local administrative capacity and moderated by office longevity. The effects persisted for decades, though the magnitude attenuated for Blacks and increased for Whites as Jim Crow deepened and local government increasingly oriented policy benefits toward Whites. The findings indicate the importance of bureaucratic organization for policy implementation and suggest the 19th‐century federal government played a larger and more successful—albeit unequal—role in citizens’ lives than commonly believed.
